The word moccasin has two main meanings as a noun. The first — and by far the most common — refers to a type of shoe. The second refers to a snake.

A moccasin is a soft, flat, flexible shoe that wraps around the foot like a glove. It is one of the simplest shoe designs in the world.

What makes it different from a regular shoe:

Most shoes you know have a firm, hard sole on the bottom — a separate thick layer that protects your foot from the ground. A moccasin is fundamentally different. In a traditional moccasin, a single piece of soft leather (or a small number of pieces) wraps up and around the entire foot — the bottom, sides, and top — all from the same material, stitched together. There is no hard, separate sole. The shoe essentially becomes a close-fitting leather pouch for your foot. This makes it extremely soft and flexible, and you can feel the ground beneath your feet quite clearly when wearing one.

Original moccasins — made by Native Americans:

Moccasins were originally created and worn by the Indigenous peoples of North America (commonly called Native Americans or American Indians). Different tribes made their own versions, but the core idea was the same: a soft leather shoe, typically made from animal hide such as deerskin, moose hide, or buffalo hide.

These shoes were not just practical — they were often works of art. Many tribes decorated their moccasins beautifully with colorful beadwork (tiny glass or shell beads sewn into patterns), porcupine quill embroidery, and painted designs. The decorations often had cultural, spiritual, or symbolic meaning specific to the tribe. You could sometimes identify which tribe a person belonged to just by looking at the style and decoration of their moccasins.

Different regions also produced different styles depending on the climate and terrain. For example, tribes in colder northern regions often made moccasins with a thick fur lining and ankle-high designs to keep feet warm in snow. Tribes in warmer, rocky regions sometimes added an extra layer of rawhide (stiff, dried animal skin) to the sole for protection, while still keeping the soft upper part.

Modern moccasins — everyday casual footwear:

Today, the word "moccasin" is used much more broadly. It refers to any casual, soft, slip-on shoe that is inspired by or loosely resembles the original Native American design. You'll find these in shoe shops worldwide, made from leather, suede, or synthetic materials. They are popular as comfortable everyday shoes, house slippers, and driving shoes.

A loafer — that flat, slip-on dress shoe — is directly descended from the moccasin design and is sometimes called a moccasin-style shoe because it shares the same foundational construction: soft leather, no lace, and a stitched seam across the top of the foot (called a moccasin stitch or apron stitch).

When people describe a shoe as having "moccasin construction," they mean the upper part of the shoe wraps under the foot and is stitched to a piece of leather on the bottom, as opposed to being glued or nailed to a hard sole.

The second meaning of moccasin is a venomous snake found in the southeastern United States. It is most commonly called the water moccasin, with its scientific name being the cottonmouth (Agkistrodon piscivorus).

It is a thick-bodied, dangerous snake that lives in and around water — swamps, marshes, rivers, and lakes. It is one of the few venomous aquatic snakes in North America. When threatened, it opens its mouth wide to display the striking white interior of its mouth, which is why it earned the nickname "cottonmouth." A bite from a water moccasin is a medical emergency.

In everyday conversation, if someone simply says "moccasin" without any other context, they almost certainly mean the shoe. The snake is nearly always referred to with the word "water" in front of it: "water moccasin."

Moccasin means a soft leather shoe that wraps around the foot, with deep roots in Native American culture, and which today describes a whole family of casual, comfortable footwear. Less commonly, it names a dangerous water snake from the American South.
